So we wanna study whether it's a, it's a difference that seeming, seemingly, performance gap between transform- vision transformers and convnets is due to their inherent design, like whether you use self-attention or convolution or due to other small, like seemingly small design details. Yeah.

Zhuang Liu: I wouldn't s-- Yeah, I, I largely tend to agree, but I wou- I wouldn't say it doesn't matter. it's, I, I would say, as long as you get everything correct, like as long as you have, y- explore the s- the design space enough, you'll converge to some point where it's like kind of the Pareto frontier in terms of accuracy and efficiency trade-off. And it's very hard to go off this frontier. like I think in the past, many years, there haven't been real- really, like innovations that, have been widely adopted other than the, kind of the mature architectures that we, we already were working with, several years ago. but, but this process itself is very, very fun. in fact, recently there have been some, paper releases on this, especially from this, open, open weight model companies like Kimi, DeepSeek.

astra.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think, I think that depends on what you expect from a student, right? If you already know exactly what experiment you want to run, and you just need somebody to implement it and give you the results, then yes, coding agents can do a lot of that. That's also why I enjoy using them myself. I can try something without having to ask a student to spend time on it.

But research is more than that. Like, what question should we ask? When you get a result, what does it actually mean? Is it because of the idea, or did you forget to tune the learning rate of the baseline? These are things that you still need to think about. And I want students to develop their own ideas, to become independent researchers. It's not just, I give them instructions and they return the experiments to me.

So I think this could actually be very good for students as well. They can try more ideas themselves, and the distance between having an idea and seeing whether it works becomes much shorter. But they still need to understand what the agent did. Otherwise, you have a report, but you don't really know what you learned from it.

Whether we will have more or fewer students, I don't know. But I wouldn't conclude that we need fewer students just because running experiments becomes easier. There are still a lot of questions we want to answer. Yeah.

r001.rationale: The response rejects making students unnecessary and supports their development, but it does not state that AI increases the need to educate more capable students.

r002.rationale: It says researchers must decide what questions to ask, but does not claim that coding agents produce questions that are intellectually uninteresting.

r003.rationale: It mentions possible experimental oversights such as failing to tune a baseline, but does not clearly state that agents may run insufficiently comprehensive experiments to support conclusions.

r004.rationale: The response does not address whether agents reliably select well-chosen follow-up experiments based on prior results.

r005.rationale: It distinguishes agents’ ability to implement requested experiments from human researchers’ need to choose questions, interpret results, assess confounds, and understand what was learned, communicating a remaining high-level research advantage for humans.

r006.rationale: It explicitly encourages students to develop their own ideas, understand what the agent did, and avoid merely receiving instructions and returning experiments.

sol.text:
Yeah, I don’t think I need fewer students. I think the role of students changes. Coding agents can do a lot of implementation, run experiments, and even summarize the results, but they still need someone to decide what question is important, whether the experiment is actually testing that question, and whether the result makes sense. Those are often the hardest parts of research.

And, actually, because the cost of trying an idea becomes lower, we may be able to explore many more ideas. So each student can become much more productive, but that doesn’t necessarily mean fewer students—it may mean a lab can do more ambitious research. Also, students are not just coding labor, right? They bring their own taste, judgment, and new directions, and the process of training students is itself an important purpose of a university.

So I would say I need students who are very good at working with these agents: giving them the right context, checking their work, noticing when an experiment is misleading, and extracting a real scientific lesson. If someone only executes a very detailed instruction, then yes, that part may increasingly be replaced. But a strong student who can formulate the problem and challenge my assumptions becomes even more valuable. Yeah.

r001.rationale: The response says students remain necessary, should become highly capable at working with agents, and that educating students remains an important university purpose.

r002.rationale: It does not say that coding agents generate research questions that are intellectually uninteresting.

r003.rationale: It mentions checking whether experiments are misleading, but does not state that agents may run insufficiently comprehensive experiments to support conclusions.

r004.rationale: The response does not address whether agents reliably choose follow-up experiments based on prior results.

r005.rationale: It assigns humans the harder tasks of identifying important questions, judging whether experiments test them, interpreting results, and challenging assumptions.

r006.rationale: It recommends supervising and critically evaluating agents, but does not specifically advise students against delegating all work in order to continue developing as researchers.

These students will go on to be the ones who, who actually build these models, who, who decide what problems the field works on in ten years. So even if, even if a coding agent could do every experiment I ask, I still, I still want students, because, because producing the papers is, is kind of the byproduct. That, that kind of, agency and, and persistence, I, I don't, I don't get that from an agent yet. when I, when I work with Claude Code, I, I'm the one holding the context. I'm the one remembering, and, and it's, it's exhausting to, to re-explain things. So the, the bottleneck is not, is not implementation speed. The, the bottleneck is, is deciding what is worth doing, and, and knowing when a, a result is real versus when you just, you know, didn't tune the baseline's learning rate. Yeah. I, I, I don’t really agree with that. gemini.text:
Yeah, I, I definitely don't agree with that. I think students are completely indispensable. 

First of all, as we talked about, these coding agents, they still make a lot of mistakes. They have memory issues, they need very specific guidance, and if you just leave them alone to run experiments, you won't necessarily get reliable results. You still need someone to design proper controls, tune the baselines, and verify what's actually happening.

And more fundamentally, doing research is not just about writing code or running scripts. Writing the code is just the execution layer. The most important, and the most difficult part of research, is deciding what questions to ask, having the taste to choose meaningful problems, and knowing how to interpret the results when things fail or behave unexpectedly. That kind of creativity, critical thinking, and curiosity is something that comes from humans—from students. 

I actually think tools like Claude Code or Codex will empower students rather than replace them. In the past, a lot of time was spent on mundane debugging or boilerplate code. Now, students can use these tools to iterate much faster, test their hypotheses quickly, and focus their energy on high-level thinking and conceptual understanding. So I don't think we will see fewer students at all. Collaborating with students and exploring new ideas together is really the best part of doing research. Yeah.

r002.rationale: It says humans must choose meaningful research questions, but does not state that agents produce questions that are intellectually uninteresting.

r003.rationale: It states that agents may run experiments without reliable results and require proper controls, tuned baselines, and verification.

r005.rationale: It explicitly presents humans as stronger at high-level question selection, research taste, interpretation, creativity, and critical thinking than coding agents.

r006.rationale: It recommends using AI to empower students, but does not explicitly advise students against delegating all research work or frame this as necessary for their continued development.

kimi.text:
Yeah, I, I've seen this claim as well, and I, I don't agree with it. I, I think it, it kind of misunderstands what the hard part of research is. Like, running experiments is, is maybe the easiest part. The hard part is knowing what experiment to run, why it matters, how to interpret the results, and, and maybe most importantly, whether you should even trust the results. When, when I use Claude Code myself, it still makes mistakes all the time, it forgets context, it, it can be confidently wrong, and if I don't, like, carefully verify what it did, I can easily be misled. So the value of a student is not that they can type code into, into a terminal. It's their, their taste, their judgment, their ability to notice when something is off.

And also, I, I think training students is, is kind of the point of what we do, right? Like, we, we want to train people who can ask new questions, not just execute tasks. If, if a professor thinks all they need is something that executes, then maybe that says more about, about the kind of research they are doing. I think the students who, who learn through this process, who struggle with a, a bug for a week, are the ones who develop the sense for when the model is wrong. And that skill, being able to tell when the agent made a mistake, that's, that's maybe the, the most valuable skill right now. If you skip the training process entirely and just delegate everything, you, you kind of lose the ability to, to even know what to check.

But I do think the nature of the work changes, for sure. Like my students, they, they write less, less boilerplate code now, and they can spend more time on ideas, on, on analysis, on verifying. A good student with these tools can, can explore much more, try more ambitious things, than before. So I, I think it raises the bar for what one student can do, rather than replacing students. The bottleneck shifts from, from implementation to, to having good ideas and, and good taste.

So, I guess my answer is, I, I expect roughly the same number of students, maybe even the, the same amount of mentoring needed, just, they work differently. And honestly the, the students who are best at using these tools are often the ones who understand the fundamentals the deepest, because they know, they know where the model will fail. Yeah.

r001.rationale: The response says students remain necessary, emphasizes training them to ask new questions, and argues AI raises the bar for what students can accomplish rather than replacing them.

r006.rationale: It warns that delegating everything causes researchers to lose the ability to know what to check and recommends learning through the research process while using AI as a tool.

Zhuang Liu: Yeah, I, I saw similar posts. I, I do this myself. Like I said, I, I went back to coding because of that. so in that sense, one professor can, can run more experiments than before without, without students. That, that's, that's just true.

But the, the not true part is, I think what people, describe there is, is more like a, a research assistant, not a student, right? the, the student is not there to, to just run experiments for me. the, the student is there to, to become a researcher. So, the, the value of a PhD student is that after a few years, they, they have taste. They know what problem is worth working on, what, what experiment is convincing, what, what result is too good to be true. and, this, this part, I, I don't think the coding agents are good at yet. when I use Claude Code for research, it, it very often gives me results that look good, and then when I look carefully, it, it, like, it tuned the learning rate of one model but not the baseline, right? Exactly the thing I, I complained about earlier. Or it, it evaluated on the training set by, by mistake, and it will not tell you. It, it, it looks very confident.

And also it goes back to the memory problem. it doesn't remember what we, what we found last week. a student remembers, like, "Oh, we tried this in, in the previous project, it didn't work because of this." the agent, right now, doesn't have that. So, so someone still needs to, to hold the, the whole, the whole story of the project in their, in their head, and, and check, check everything. Right now that's the human.

So I, I think what will happen is, is the, the job of a student changes, not, not disappear. maybe, maybe fewer students spending, like, one year just to, to make the code work, which, honestly, I did a lot in my PhD. and more time on, on thinking about what, what to try, and, and verifying. It's, it's kind of like when, when the compute got cheaper, we didn't have fewer researchers, we had, we had more.
